deleted.text: This note describes how the newsroom site caches rendered HTML pages at the content delivery edge.
It covers what is cached, how the cache key is formed, how long a page stays fresh, and what editors should expect after they publish.
The goal is to keep origin load flat during traffic spikes while letting readers see corrections within a predictable time.
Personalised responses are marked private by the origin and pass through the edge untouched.
The cache key is the normalised path plus the consent flag.
The normaliser lowercases the host, strips tracking parameters such as utm_source, and sorts the remaining query parameters.
Many sites vary cached pages by the full cookie header.
Our pages read only the consent cookie, so the key carries that one flag and nothing else from the request headers.
Every rendered page is cached at the edge with a fixed 300-second TTL.
The publishing system sends no purges to the edge, so a changed page reaches readers only when its cached copy expires at each edge location.
We call the period between a publish and the moment every edge location has refetched the page the staleness window.
The staleness window never exceeds 300 seconds, and editors, support staff and the corrections desk all plan around that figure.
Browsers receive a client lifetime of 60 seconds in the response headers, which comes on top of the staleness window.

The origin sets all three directives on every cacheable response.
The edge configuration holds no lifetimes of its own, so a change to any of them is a change to the origin.
The origin starts rendering the new version for any request that reaches it.
Each edge location keeps serving its cached copy until the 300-second TTL runs out there.
The next request at that location fetches the new version from the origin and caches it again.
Editors who need to check a correction wait out the staleness window before reloading the live page.
The corrections desk adds five minutes to every promised correction time it gives to readers or to legal.
Embargoed stories are scheduled to publish at the embargo time.
A new URL is never in the cache, so it appears at once, but any update made after it goes live is subject to the staleness window like any other change.
The origin is sized for the refetch load that follows a full expiry cycle, which on a normal weekday peaks at about 350 requests per second.

The web platform team owns the edge configuration and the origin headers.
Changes to cache rules go through a pull request reviewed by one platform engineer and one newsroom product owner.

candidates.sentence: The edge never stores a response that carries a session cookie or an authorisation header.
The key is derived from the request alone rather than from a hash of the rendered page body.
We do not vary by cookies beyond the consent flag, because no other cookie changes what our rendered pages contain.
A corrected headline therefore reaches readers when the publish commits, not whenever a cached copy happens to run out.
Purging by URL would not work for us, because one article appears on dozens of section fronts and listing pages.
Purge requests travel over that authenticated API, not through any shared message queue that other teams could write to.
When the tag header is missing from an origin response, the edge passes the page through without storing it.
The edge configuration holds no lifetimes of its own, so a change to any of them is a change to the origin.
A purge never reaches those browsers, and their copies are bounded only by the short client lifetime set by the origin.
An editor who has just published can reload the live page straight away instead of holding off before checking it.
A new URL is never in the cache, so it appears at once, and later updates are purged like any other change.
There is no staleness window to account for when scheduling an embargoed story.
